*Mingbao ji* (Records of Karmic Retribution): Compiled Volume One.
Zhou Min of the Jin dynasty was a native of Jiangnan and served as the Protector-General (Hujun Jiangjun) of the Jin. His family had followed the Dharma for generations.

During the rebellion of Su Jun, the people of the capital were all displaced, migrating east and west. Hearing that his family possessed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin), they transcribed it onto a single roll of eight-zhang silk, writing over and over again until the entire text was complete.
They also had several other scriptures in multiple volumes, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* was interspersed among them. As they were then facing the perils of flight...
He set out, unable to carry them all away. He reproached the various *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Dapin) texts, not knowing which ones were inside which tower.

Being in a hurry to depart, he did not have time to search through them thoroughly; he paced back and forth in lamentation, unaware that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* suddenly emerged from outside on its own.

Overcome with both pity and joy, he took it away. The Zhou family has thus treasured it as a family heirloom for generations. It is now said that it still exists today. One account states that it was the wife of Zhou Song, named Humu.
There was a large scroll of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* written on silk five inches wide, upon which one entire volume of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* was inscribed.
Wang Fan, the Magistrate of Fuyang County during the Jin dynasty, had a concubine named Taoying who possessed extraordinary beauty.

She subsequently engaged in illicit affairs with two men, Ding Feng and Shi Huaqi, both of whom were attendants of the palace. While Wang Fan was away on an official journey and had not yet returned, Sun Yuanbi, the Commander of the Inner Quarters, heard [of this].
Ding Feng heard the sound of tinkling jade ornaments within the room and peered inside. He saw Tao Ying lying in the same bed as him.
Yuanbi knocked on the door and shouted at them; Tao Ying immediately rose, adjusted her skirt and smoothed her hair, and stepped out wearing her slippers back into the inner quarters.
Yuanbi also noticed that Huaqi was wearing Tao Ying’s musk scent upon his belt. Fearing that Yuanbi would report their misconduct, the two of them conspired to slander him.

He had a secret affair with Tao Ying. Because Fan did not investigate the matter, he subsequently killed Yuanbi. At that time, a man named Chen Chao was present at the scene and incited Yuanbi’s crime.
Later, when Fan returned from his mission abroad, Chao also went to the capital to see him. As they were traveling beneath Mount Chiting, they encountered a thunderstorm.
When night fell, a person suddenly appeared, took Chao by the armpit, and dragged him straight away into the Eight Wildernesses.

In the midst of a marsh, a flash of lightning illuminated the scene. A ghost appeared with a face that was intensely blue-black; its eyes were devoid of pupils. It said, "I am Yuanbi, the grandson of Wang.

I have appealed my grievance to the August Heaven; may it be adjudicated soon. I have been waiting for you for some time, and now we have met. Chao prostrated himself until blood flowed from his forehead.
The ghost said, "Since Wang Fan is the mastermind of this matter, he should be killed first. [Next are] Jia Jingbo and Sun Wen."

Dù was at the Xuántáng (Mysterious Hall) below Mount Tàishān, where they together compiled the registers of names for the living and the dead. The souls of the peach blossoms were also taken into the Nǚqīng Studio.
When dawn arrived, they lost track of the ghosts' whereabouts. Sòng Chāo went to the capital of Yáng and visited Fǎn, yet he did not dare to thank him.
He then saw a ghost coming from outside and entering Fan’s tent directly. At night, when Fan had finally fallen asleep, he was suddenly struck by a severe nightmare;
he called out repeatedly but did not wake up. His family members brought a blue ox to Fan’s side and applied peachwood figurines and left-hand cords.
By dawn, he had slightly recovered, but died after ten days. His concubine also died suddenly. Chao then fled to Changqian Temple, where he changed his character and name.
For what reason? Five years later, on the third day of the second month, while drinking wine by the water, Chao said, "From now on, I shall no longer fear this ghost.
As he lowered his head, he saw the shadow of the ghost already within the water.
It struck Chao’s nose with its hand, and blood gushed forth in a quantity of about one *sheng*. He died several days later.
The Śramaṇa Senggui of the Song dynasty was a monk of Wudang Temple. At that time, Zhang Yu of Jingzhao frequently invited Senggui to his home in this county to receive offerings.
On the fifth day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Yongchu era, he suddenly died without any prior illness.
After two days, he revived and recounted his experience, saying: "In the second watch of the night on the fifth, I heard a clamorous sound from between the gate and the alleyway."
There was a clamorous noise. In a short while, five men appeared, holding bright torches and banners of faith, coming straight into the house.
They shouted at Senggui, who then collapsed and fell into a daze. The five men immediately bound him with red ropes and led him away.
As they traveled, they reached a mountain entirely devoid of grass or trees; the soil was hard and black, resembling stone or iron. On both sides of the mountain were white bones.
It was filled with accumulated earth. After traveling several tens of li through the mountains, they reached a three-way fork.

There stood a man, very tall and robust, clad in armor and holding a staff, who asked, "Of the five of you, how many have come? They replied, "Only one. The five then intended to enter one of the paths.
Suddenly, they arrived at a city; outside were dozens of houses built of rammed earth, with wooden posts standing before each dwelling.
It was over ten *zhang* in length and had iron beams upon it, shaped like wedge-shaped water-lifting devices (*kegao*). On the left and right were caskets for holding earth;
the earth came in various quantities, some in the form of ten *hu*, and others as large as five *sheng*. There was one man whose robes and cap were both red.
The official said, "When you were born into this world, what sins or merits did you possess? Speak according to the truth; do not speak falsely.
Guī was terrified and did not answer. A man in red clothing, like a clerk of the bureau, said, "We may open the registers and examine your sins and merits.
After a short while, the clerk arrived beneath a tall tree, carrying a chest of earth which he suspended from an iron beam to weigh it. It seemed as though the scale tilted up and down.
The official said to Gui, "This is the scale for weighing merit and transgression. Your merit is slight while your transgressions are many; you ought to undergo punishment first.
Suddenly, there was a man dressed in the robes of a high official who said to Gui, "You are a śramaṇa; why do you not recite the Buddha's name?"
"I have heard that by repenting one's transgressions, one may be delivered from the eight difficulties. Let us therefore concentrate our minds together to invoke the Buddha.
The official said to the man: "You may invoke him for this person as well. Since he is a disciple of the Buddha, it would be fortunate if he were granted deliverance.

The official then once again placed the scale upon the beam and invoked the name; the scale then became perfectly level. Subsequently, they brought Gui before the supervising official to settle the matter. The supervising official—
He took up his brush and examined the registers, hesitating for a long time. Then another man appeared, dressed in crimson robes and a black cap, wearing a seal and carrying a jade tablet.
He came forward and said, "This person's name does not yet appear upon the registers of the reckoning. The supervising official was startled and ordered the man on the right to record him.
A moment later, five people were seen being brought in bound hand and foot. The supervising official asked, "O ghosts of execution, why do you bring these in indiscriminately?"
They brought the man and whipped him. After a short while, a messenger arrived, saying that the Heavenly Emperor had summoned the practitioner.
Upon arriving at the imperial palace, he observed that everything was composed of gold and jewels; their brilliant radiance was so dazzling that one could not look upon it steadily.
The Emperor’s attendants wore crimson robes and jeweled crowns adorned with exquisite treasures. The Emperor said, "You are a śramaṇa; why do you not apply yourself diligently to your practice?"
He had been unjustly captured by a minor spirit. Senggui bowed his head to the Buddhas and prayed for blessings.
The Emperor said, "Your life is not yet exhausted; you shall now return to life. You should apply yourself diligently to spiritual cultivation and must no longer frequent the homes of laypeople.
Spirits who kill people often commit wrongful excesses, such as those involving someone like you. Senggui asked, "By what means may one be rescued from the calamity of such wrongful excess?"
He was exempted from it. The Emperor said, "To extensively establish meritorious works is most excellent. If you cannot manage that, you may instead observe the Eight Precepts (Aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa).
This will ensure that while alive you avoid calamities, and when dead you shall leave behind the hells; this is also a worthy alternative. Having finished speaking, he sent Daogui away.
Not long after his departure, [Daogui] saw a monastery with many śramaṇas; there he encountered the disciple of Master Bai, the abbot of Wudang Temple.

Huijin was present at all these locations. His residence was grand and orderly, and his provisions were naturally abundant. Dao Gui requested to dwell there. A certain śramaṇa said, "This is a ground of merit;
it is not a place for you to occupy. The messenger returned with Dao Gui to the home of Yu and departed.
He Danzhi was a native of Donghai and served as the Grand Minister of Agriculture during the Song dynasty. He did not believe in the scriptures and frequently committed acts of cruelty.
Hài suffered from an illness during the Yongchu era. He saw a ghost whose form was extremely tall and robust, with an ox’s head and a human body.

It held an iron fork in its hand and guarded him day and night. Distraught and terrified, he had Daoist practitioners compose ritual texts, talismans, seals, and registers, and performed every kind of exorcism and protective rite;
yet the apparition appeared just as before. His acquaintance, the śramaṇa Huìyì, heard of his illness and went to visit him. [Huìyì] calmly... for him.
He described what he had seen. Huiyi said, "This is the ox-headed *āpāra* (hell-warden). Sin and merit are never obscured; they are summoned solely by those who invite them.
If you can turn your mind toward the Dharma, this ghost will naturally vanish. Yet your delusion remains deep and your nature has not been transformed.
Shortly thereafter, he died. (The above account is verified in the *Mingxiang ji*).
Sima Wenxuan of the Song dynasty was a native of Henei. He was a devoted believer in the Dharma.

In the ninth year of the Yuanjia era, while observing the mourning period for his deceased younger brother, he suddenly beheld his brother on the morning of the full moon at the shrine. His physical form appeared no different from when he was alive;
he paced about, sighing with lamentation, and requested food and drink. Wen then tested him by speaking, saying: "During your lifetime, you practiced the ten virtuous deeds."
"If, as the sutras say, one should attain rebirth in heaven, and if he were in the human realm, why has he been born among these ghosts?

When Wenxuan spoke thus, the ghost bowed its head and remained silent, offering no reply. That evening, Wenxuan dreamed of his younger brother, who said, "Regarding the good deeds I cultivated while alive, I have received the retribution of being born in heaven.
The ghost at the spirit altar this morning was merely a demon chieftain; it was not my true self. I fear you, elder brother..."
Finding this strange and suspicious, he went to inform his elder brother. The next morning, Prince Wenxuan invited monks to recite the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and ordered men to seize and bind him.
The ghost then fled beneath the bed and further ran outside the door; its form was somewhat hideous, and the entire family was struck with terror, reviling and shouting at it to depart.
The ghost said, "I am but a hungry beggar seeking food. After several days had passed, it finally left. Shortly thereafter, by the mother’s spirit-bed...

Upon his head there was a ghost, its skin and body red in color, and its form exceedingly tall and robust. Wenxuan sighed deeply. Xiaozu conversed with it back and forth; the responses were complete and thorough.
Although he was initially terrified, in the end he gradually became accustomed to it. The ghost, in turn, grew increasingly familiar and intimate with him.
In their dwelling and their comings and goings, they were almost like members of the same family. At that time, the news spread throughout the capital, and people came and went to observe them.

The doorways and alleys were filled with crowds of people following one after another. At that time, there was a monk at Nanlin Temple who, along with the śramaṇa Senghan of Lingwei Temple, engaged in very detailed and intimate conversation with a ghost.
The ghost said, "In a previous life, I was once a person of noble status, but because I committed many evils, my retribution remains incomplete, and thus I have received this ghostly body.
In the year of the Tiger, four hundred classes of ghosts will spread a great epidemic."

Regarding the calamity of Yingzhong: it does not concern the practitioners of the Way; rather, it concerns those who commit transgressions and excesses while falsely claiming to possess merit and goodness.
Therefore, I have come to oversee them. The monk offered food to him, but the ghost said, "I already have my own provisions; I cannot accept this food.
Fayuan asked, "The ghosts know much about my life—where did I come from, and for what reason did I become a practitioner? The ghost replied, "A human being..."

He came from within [the realm of spirits]. His reasons for leaving the household life were rooted in his original vows. He was questioned regarding the living and the dead, and their destinies in birth and death;

he answered briefly yet completely, and his responses were possessed of spiritual efficacy. As the details are numerous, they are not recorded here in full. Huan said: "The paths of humans and ghosts are distinct."
"You have not sought food; why do you linger so long? The ghost replied, "There is a woman here who ought to be captured.

Because she is diligent in observing the precepts, she is difficult to obtain. It is for this reason that I have delayed these past days; I feel no small amount of shame before my host for causing such disturbance.
From that time forward, he did not appear very often. Later, those who went to look for him heard only—

He spoke thus. It was the tenth year of the Yuanjia era. On the twenty-eighth day of the third month, he said to Wénxuān, "I have come for a brief stay, but you have mobilized your entire household to cultivate merit. Since you view me with such dread, how can I remain long? Xiàozǔ said:
"I will allow you to stay as a guest. Why have you taken over the spirit altar of one who has already passed away? He replied, "The deceased in your family each have their own designated places;
this seat is set out empty, so I am merely staying here temporarily. Thereupon, he took his leave.
Song Wang Hu was a native of Chang’an. Several years after his uncle had died, in the twenty-third year of the Yuanjia era, the uncle suddenly appeared in person.
He returned home to reprimand Wang Hu for failing to maintain proper decorum and for neglecting household affairs, and he punished him with five strokes of the cane.
Those nearby and the neighbors all heard his words and the sound of the blows, and they even saw the marks left by the caning, yet they did not see his form.
Only Hu was still permitted to approach him intimately. The elder brother said to Hu, "I ought not to die; the Way of the Spirits requires me to calculate the registers of the various ghosts.
Now, with such a great retinue of officials and soldiers, I fear they might alarm and damage the villages; therefore, I have not brought them forward.

Hu also saw the multitude of ghosts outside the village, bustling and clamorous. Suddenly, the elder brother took his leave, saying, "I shall return next year on the seventh day of the seventh month."
"In a short while, I shall return again. I wish to take you on a journey through the dark paths so that you may come to know the retribution of sin and merit.
There is no need for elaborate preparations; if your mind is not yet at rest, you need only come with me. When he reached this point, he indeed returned and said to the Hu family members:
"I have now finished taking the Hu man on his tour of observation; I shall send him back, so there is no need for concern. The Hu man then lay down and fell asleep immediately.
On the bed, he was completely submerged as if having vanished. Thereupon, Shu took Hu and toured the surrounding mountains, where they witnessed various ghosts and monsters in full detail.

Before they reached Mount Songgao, the ghosts passed by Hu, and for each of them, a meal was prepared; the flavors provided were no different from those in the human world, except that the ginger was exceptionally crisp and delicious.
Hu wished to take some with him when returning, but the attendants laughed at him and said, "This is merely food for the moment; it cannot be taken away."
He was permitted to return. On the way back, he saw a place where the buildings were magnificent and spacious, and the curtains and mats were elegantly arranged;
two young monks resided there. He approached them, and the two monks provided him with various fruits, betel nuts, and other refreshments. He remained wandering through that area for a long time.

Having fully witnessed the retributions of sin and merit, as well as suffering and joy, he took his leave and returned home. His uncle said to Hu, "Since you already know that goodness is to be cultivated, why should you remain at home?
The *āraṇyaka* with white feet possesses refined and lofty observance of the precepts; he is worthy to be served as a teacher.
Because this Daoist from Chang'an had white feet, people of the time called him the "White-footed *Āraṇyaka*. He was highly esteemed by the Wei barbarians.

The barbarian ruler treated him with reverence and served him as his teacher. Once the barbarian had received these instructions, he went to that monastery and saw a young monk from Mount Song traveling among the assembly.
The barbarian was greatly surprised and greeted him after their long separation, asking when he had arrived. The two monks replied, "We originally resided in this monastery;

we do not recall ever having known you in the past. The barbarian spoke again: [...]* *Note: The original Chinese text provided here is incomplete at the end. The translation reflects the available portion.*
Regarding the encounter at Mount Songgao, this monk said, "Your Lordship is mistaken; how could such a thing exist? The next day, the two monks departed without a word.
Hu then informed the various śramaṇas and recounted what he had seen at Mount Songgao in the past.

The assembly was all struck with wonder and immediately searched for the two monks, but they were nowhere to be found; thus, they realized they were divine beings. This occurred at the end of the Yuanjia era.
There was a monk from Chang’an named Shi Tanshuang who traveled to Jiangnan and recounted these matters in detail.
Li Dan of the Song dynasty, whose courtesy name was Shize, was a native of Guangling. He was renowned in his hometown for his filial piety, prudence, and simple integrity.

On the fourteenth day of the first month in the third year of the Yuanjia era, he died suddenly; however, the area below his heart did not grow cold. After seven days, he revived. [They] placed [a substance] in his mouth...
He drank some congee. After one night, he returned to his normal state and said: "There was a man carrying a banner of faith who came to the head of my bed and announced, 'The Prefect summons you.

At dawn, I followed him. We traveled straight toward the north; the road was very level and clean. Upon reaching the city, the towers and pavilions were as magnificent as those of the imperial palace today.
He sent a messenger with instructions to offer me consolation and inquire after me, saying, 'You may proceed forward. I saw him upon the great hall."

There were thirty men, wearing single-layered robes and blue headbands, seated in a solemn, forest-like array. One man sat facing east, clad in a long robe and leaning against a desk, with some one hundred attendants standing guard on his left and right.
Looking at the dawn, he spoke to those seated there, saying, "I shall show you the various hells so that the world may know them.
As soon as they heard these words, they raised their heads and looked in all directions; everything they had previously seen had vanished, and it was now indeed hell.
In the midst [of his vision], he saw a multitude of sinners undergoing various retributive sufferings; their groans and cries were unbearable to behold.
Soon, a messenger of the teachings appeared and said, "Lord Fu and Lord Xin, you may return; we shall welcome you again later. Thereupon, they returned.
In the first month of the sixth year, he died once more, and after seven days, he revived again. He recounted the events he had witnessed, roughly as before. Among them were certain prisoners...

He sent word back to his family, saying, "I have committed a crime while alive; please perform meritorious deeds on my behalf. He then spoke somewhat of his surname, name, relatives, and place of residence.
When they searched for him according to these instructions, they found him. Furthermore, he said, "In the year Jiashen, a pestilence shall spread and kill many wicked people.
Disciples of the Buddha who observe the Eight Precepts (Bā-kuān-zhāi), restrain themselves, cultivate their minds, and practice wholesome deeds may escape it. At dawn—

He served as a Daoist *jijiu* (libationer). Initially, he intended to discard the records and follow his own methods; however, because the Daoist laity remonstrated against him, he ultimately pursued both paths.
He constantly exhorted others to practice the Eight Precepts Retreat (*bāguānzhāi*).

Zheng Xianzhi of Yingyang, who served as the Minister of the Interior (Shangshu Puye) under the Song dynasty, was traveling with the Imperial Carriage on an inspection tour of the capital in the fourth year of the Yuanjia era.
Upon arriving at the capital, he died suddenly that evening. His spirit then spoke to those around him, saying: "My lifespan had long since been exhausted, and I should have passed away long ago.

However, because I have respectfully believed in the Buddha-dharma, practiced releasing living beings, and made offerings during these recent years, I have been able to extend my life for several more years by virtue of this merit."

Now, the retribution between the hidden and the manifest is as certain as a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound. One ought to cast aside worldly affairs and elevate the mind toward the Great Teaching.

At that time, many of the eminent and noble heard it said that the Śramaṇa Fazang of Baoshi Monastery in Fu Prefecture of the Sui dynasty was pure and refined in his observance of the precepts, and by nature upright and straightforward. During the Sui dynasty...
In the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era, he established a monastery at Weichuan City in Luojiao County. Its Buddha hall was exquisite and its monks’ quarters magnificent;

sacred images, banners, and flowers were all fully provided. In the fifth year of the Daye era, by imperial decree, monasteries and stupas were consolidated and sent to the great monasteries of the prefectures.
Among those that were destroyed, Master [Dao]zang repaired and restored them all, constructing halls to house them.

Setting this aside, he also produced all the scriptures; he had already transcribed eight hundred fascicles. Fearing that his home province lacked skilled scribes, paper, and brushes, he went to the capital’s former Yue’ai Temple to copy them.
By the intercalary second month of the second year of the Wude era, he fell ill for over twenty days.
Thereupon, he saw a person dressed in fine blue robes standing atop a high pavilion, holding a scripture in their hand.

He addressed the Dharma-treasury, saying: "Since you first took up this body, although you have performed great meritorious deeds, all of which were refined and sublime, there remains only a small portion of mutual misappropriation of the property of the Triple Gem, for which you have incurred immeasurable sin. That which I now hold is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
If you can personally transcribe one scroll of it, it will cause all the sins incurred from your use of the property of the Triple Gem to be completely extinguished."
At that time, the Tripitaka Master replied immediately: "Although I have transcribed other sutras, I have not yet transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
I only pray that my illness may be cured so that I may not dare disobey your command. Now that you have awakened me, I, your disciple, possess no other things."
He possessed nothing but his three robes, alms bowl, shoulder-cloth, and *saṃkakṣikā*, all of which he entrusted to a virtuous elder and his disciples.
He also produced one hundred fascicles of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Within three or five days, as his life was about to end, he beheld Amitābha Buddha coming to welcome him.
By the power of these scriptures, he attained rebirth in the Western Land and did not enter the three miserable realms.
Śramaṇa Huíyún of Dōngchuān during the Sui dynasty was a native of Fányáng. He entered the monastic order at the age of twelve and devoted himself to traveling to study under various masters.

When he reached the age of eighteen, he was riding a donkey when he stopped at his uncle’s house. His uncle, seeing that the donkey was swift, intended to kill it; he happened to be carrying a knife as he went toward it.
He saw a man in yellow robes beneath the eastern wall who raised his fist and shouted back at him, saying, "This practitioner is about to become a Great Superior who penetrates the Dharma;
how can you bear to wish to harm him? Terrified, the elder brother informed his wife. His wife said, "Your mind was not firm; it was merely caused by optical illusion.
Having heard this, he went there again and once more saw a man in yellow robes beneath the western wall who said, "Do not kill the practitioner. If you kill him..."
