The monk prostrated himself, saying, "I beg you to spare my life; I swear by a vow never to speak of this for the rest of my days. The Emperor Wen-zong killed him and cast his body away among the weeds.
After more than twenty days, as he was returning from his journey, he passed by the place where the monk had died. It was the height of summer, and he suspected the body must have rotted away.
He went to look and found it remained exactly as it had been when alive. Zong dismounted and struck the monk’s mouth with his riding crop;
a fly emerged from the mouth, buzzing clearly as it flew straight into Zong’s nose. It remained there for a long time without emerging, causing him great distress. After more than a year, [he died].
Death.
Du Tongda, a native of Gaoyuan County in Qizhou during the Tang dynasty, was ordered by the county magistrate in the Zhenguan era to escort a monk northward.
Upon seeing the monk’s scripture box, Tongda remarked, "It is all filled with silk and brocade," and then [discussed it] with his wife.
Together they struck and killed the monk. While the monk was still not dead, he recited two or three phrases of a mantra.

Immediately, a fly flew into his nose and remained there for a long time without emerging. His eyes and nose became congested, his eyebrows and beard suddenly fell out, and he became so bewildered that he lost his way and his spirit was utterly despondent.
Before long, he contracted a malignant disease and died within a year. As he lay on his deathbed...
At the end, a fly flew out and entered his wife’s nose. His wife fell ill and died after more than a year.
During the Zhenguan era, Lu Xiaozheng of Yongzhou served as the Left Fruit Yi of the Xichuan Commandery in the Right Guard.
By nature, Xiaozheng was impetuous and frequently committed acts of cruelty. Previously, there had been a hive of honeybees within the commandery, which had split and flown away in groups.
On a tree to the south of the residence, Xiao Zheng then sent someone to move the bees to a separate niche.

While the bees had not yet departed, Xiao Zheng became greatly enraged; he subsequently boiled a basin of hot water and poured it over the bees on the tree, so that they all died, with hardly a single offspring left behind.
In the fifth month of the following year, while Xiao Zheng was napping in his hall, a bee suddenly stung him.
His tongue became swollen and obstructed his mouth; he died after several days.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a woman surnamed Liang in Xianyang who died and returned to life seven days later. She said of herself:
She was taken by her captors into a large courtyard where she saw a great hall. There sat an official at his desk holding a pen, surrounded by a grand retinue of attendants.
He ordered an interrogation, asking: "Should this woman be put to death or not?

Someone else brought forward another case, stating that the woman shared the same name as one who was destined for execution; therefore, she had been summoned. The official issued a command to the left.
The man was about to release him when Liang addressed the official, saying, "I do not know what other offenses I may have committed.

I request that I accept my punishment and return home. The official then ordered an investigation of the records, which stated: "Throughout his life, Liang has committed nothing but the sins of double-tongued speech and foul abuse;
there are no other crimes. Thereupon, the official ordered one man to pull out his tongue and another to seize an axe and chop it off. This occurred daily.

This occurred four times, lasting a total of seven days before he was finally sent back home. Initially, it felt as though he had fallen down a deep precipice; after a short while, he awoke from what seemed like sleep.
When his family examined his tongue, they found it was still extensively ulcerated and swollen. From that time forward, he permanently renounced alcohol and meat, a practice he maintains to this day.

Fu Yi, the Director of the Bureau of Astronomy during the Tang dynasty, was originally a native of Taiyuan. At the end of the Sui dynasty, he moved to Fufeng. From his youth, he was fond of extensive learning;

he was skilled in astronomy, calendrical science, and mathematics. He was quick-witted and eloquent, capable of engaging in spirited debate. For approximately twenty years, from the Wude to the Zhenguan eras, he served as the Director of the Bureau of Astronomy.
By nature, he did not believe in the Buddha-dharma and frequently held the monastics and nuns in contempt, even using stone statues for bricks and tiles.
...for use. In the autumn of the fourteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he died suddenly of illness.
Initially, Yi, along with his companions Fu Renjun and Xue Ze, all served as Directors of the Bureau of Astronomy. Before Renjun had repaid five thousand coins he owed to Ze, Renjun passed away.
Subsequently, Ze dreamed of Renjun, who spoke to him as usual. Ze said, "Because of the money I previously owed you..."
"To whom shall it be entrusted? Renjun replied, "It may be entrusted to the person of Nili. Zeli asked, "Who is this Nili person?
He answered, "It is Fu Yi, the Director of the Bureau of Astronomy. Upon waking, that same night, Feng Changming, the Supervisor of the Office of Imperial Manufactories, also had a dream.
"I have frequently encountered deceased persons in one place who, while long-lived, heard the scriptures explain the retribution of sins and blessings.

I do not yet know whether this must necessarily exist. He replied, "It exists entirely. Again he asked, "As for someone like Fu Yi, who did not believe during his lifetime—what retribution will he receive after death?
He replied, "Sins and blessings certainly exist; however, Fu Yi has already been banished to Yuezhou."

He was a person from the *niraya* (the term *niraya* is translated according to the sutras as "Avīci," the Great Hell of Uninterrupted Suffering). With a long life, he entered the palace one morning and saw Sengze.

He then recounted his dream, and Sengze in turn described the matters concerning those in the *niraya*. The two of them, during the same night in the darkness, found their accounts to correspond perfectly.
Together they sighed in admiration, saying that the matters of sin and merit must not be disbelieved. Having witnessed these signs, Sengze then sent him back.
He gave the money to Yi and recounted his dream to him. A few days later, Yi suddenly passed away.

On the day of his initial death, there were many ominous signs that cannot be described in detail. When [the deceased] was brought before the court, he personally saw two officials; their accounts of the dream were identical.
He was a native of Zou County in Yanzhou during the Tang dynasty; his surname was Zhang, and his courtesy name is unknown. He had previously served as a county magistrate.

In the sixteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he intended to travel to the capital to participate in the imperial examinations. On his way, he passed through Mount Tai and visited the temple to pray for blessings.

Within the temple, the Lord of the Shrine, his consort, and their various sons all manifested their physical forms. After Zhang had finished prostrating himself before each of them in turn, he came before the fourth son.
Observing from the side that his appearance was elegant and handsome, Zhang alone made a vow to his five traveling companions:

"If only I could become friends with this fourth brother, composing poetry and raising cups throughout our lives—what need would there be for official service? After they had traveled several li, suddenly dozens of horsemen arrived brandishing their whips.
His attendants said it was the Fourth Brother. The Fourth Brother said, "I saw you just now, elder brother, hanging [your head]..."

Yin came specifically to pay his respects and said, "I understand that you, my elder brother, intend to take the examinations; however, this year it is not auspicious for you to obtain an official post.
Furthermore, I fear there will be calamities ahead on your journey, so you need not go. Zhang did not follow his advice and took his leave.
After traveling more than a hundred li, Zhang and his companions were robbed by bandits during their night journey, and all their belongings were plundered.
It was exhausted. Zhang Su then offered a prayer, saying, "Fourth Brother, will you not assist us? After a short while, Fourth Brother’s chariot and cavalry arrived in full.
They were struck with amazement for a long time, and he immediately ordered his attendants to pursue the thieves. The thieves, dazed and confused, fled back to their original location.
Fourth Brother ordered men to flog them several dozen times; the thieves' thighs and calves were all mangled and raw, after which they departed. Fourth Brother pointed—
There was a great tree. It was here that they called out to one another on the day the elder brother returned. That year, Zhang Guo failed to obtain an official post and returned home.
Upon reaching the designated spot, he called out loudly for "Fourth Brother. In an instant, the latter arrived. He then led Zhang away, saying, "Follow me across the residence.
Immediately, there appeared soaring towers and ornate pavilions stretching across the distance and soaring into the void; their battlements were staggered and exceptionally magnificent. Attendants...

Wei Zhongzhi’s residence was as magnificent as that of a sovereign. Once Zhang Ji had entered the inner quarters, the Fourth Brother immediately said, "One must first pay respects to the Lord of the Prefecture before one may sit at ease.
He then led Zhang inside; they passed through more than ten successive gates, proceeding with hurried steps until they reached the base of the great hall.

There, Zhang paid his respects to the Lord of the Prefecture, who appeared exceptionally majestic and extraordinary. At that moment, Zhang was so overcome with trepidation that he did not dare look up.
He looked at it; the official’s judgment on the case appeared to be written in vermilion ink, and the characters were all large. The Prefect ordered his attendant to announce:
"Since you are able to associate with my son, this is truly a path of great virtue. You should stay for one or two days for a banquet; you may leave as you please after that.
He then had him led out to a separate pavilion, where delicacies from both land and sea were lavishly prepared in full array, and the music of stringed and bamboo instruments began to play.
The sounds of music and singing filled his ears. He then went to sleep in the same room as the Fourth Brother.
After one night had passed, Zhang Zhi set out for a stroll through the courtyard the following morning, pacing back and forth.

He then peered into a courtyard and saw his wife standing before a group of officials with a cangue upon her head. Zhang returned to the hall, feeling deeply displeased. The Fourth Brother questioned him in wonderment.
Zhang explained the circumstances in detail. The Fourth Brother was greatly startled and said, "I did not know my sister-in-law had come here.

He immediately went in person to the various judicial offices. There were some dozens of such officials there; seeing the Fourth Brother arrive, they all ran down the steps and stood with their hands pressed together in awe.
He beckoned one official forward with his hand and related this matter in full. The official replied:
"I dare not disobey your command; however, I must inform the Registrar. He then summoned the Registrar, who consented and said, "Furthermore, this case must be filed together with other cases.
Only by skillfully joining it with the others can it be adjudicated. The Judicial Officer then ruled: "This woman’s case has been investigated separately.
She possesses the merit of having transcribed scriptures and observed the fasts; it is not appropriate to [punish her] immediately."
He died. [The King] then released him and allowed him to return home. Zhang and Siliang wept as they parted;

Zhang established a memorial for him and further instructed Zhang, saying, "Only by performing meritorious deeds can one increase one's lifespan. Zhang mounted his own horse, while his wife borrowed a horse from Siliang, and they returned together.
Although his wife’s spirit remained as if she were in her usual state, when they were about to reach their home, they were still some hundred paces away from the house.
Suddenly she vanished. Zhang was seized with great terror and fled home. There he encountered his son and daughter weeping; he learned that she had already been interred.
Zhang immediately called his children and hurried to open the coffin. Upon opening it, he saw his wife suddenly rise and sit up.
She laughed heartily and said, "I missed my children, so do not be alarmed that I departed first. Thus, after having been dead for six or seven days, she returned to life.
This is what the local people of Yanzhou have said.
*Mingbao ji jishu*, Scroll Three;
*Mingbao ji jishu*, Scroll Four.
Li Zhili of Longxi in the Tang dynasty was agile from his youth and skilled in archery. He was also adept at riding and practiced the art of shooting pellets, killing many enemies.
On occasion, he would net fish in numbers beyond counting. In the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he fell slightly ill and died within three or four days.
Thereupon, he saw a ghost leading a horse that was larger than any horse commonly ridden in the secular world.
Zhilü said, "King Yama is pursuing you. He then ordered Zhilü to mount a horse, and in a mere moment, they suddenly arrived before the King.
The King issued a command, saying, "I have sent you to subdue the rebels; you must not suffer defeat. Should you fail, I shall put you to death.
There were twenty-four companions with him who looked toward the northeast; they could see no end to the rebels, as heaven and earth were completely shrouded in darkness and dust.

It rained down upon them. Zhili and his companions were defeated. He said to those traveling with him, "The King’s instructions are severe; it would be better to die advancing forward than to return in defeat.
Zhili turned his horse back and shot three arrows ahead. Thereafter, the bandits seemed to retreat slightly.

When the number of shots reached five, the bandits were finally routed and dispersed. Having finished the task, he went to see the King. The King rebuked Zhili, saying, "Even though your enemy has retreated, why..."
At the time of the first battle, they were defeated immediately. Their hair was braided with hemp, their hands and feet were bound, and they were laid upon stones and crushed by heavy boulders.
The bodies of four men in succession were completely mangled and rotted away. When it was Zhi-li’s turn, he cried out in a defiant voice:
"The enemy's defeat just now was entirely due to the power of Zhi-li; yet I am now being killed by the king—there is no way to be defiant!"
Afterwards, the king released him, leaving him with no further attachments. He roamed at will for three days, when he traveled toward the northwest and entered a walled enclosure.
There was a pack of beasts filling more than three *mu* of ground, all of whom came to claim his life, gradually closing in on him.
He had once shot and killed a female dog, which now came straight forward and bit his face, then proceeded to his body.
His entire body was without exception wounded. He saw three great ghosts, each one chiang and five chi tall, with a girth equal to their height.

Together they flayed his skin and flesh until, in a mere moment, it was entirely gone; only his face, eyes, and white bones remained, as well as his internal organs. They then divided this flesh to give to birds and beasts;
as soon as the flesh fell away, it grew back again, and once grown, it was flayed once more. This continued in this manner for three [days].
The day was spent in such extreme agony that it could not be fully recorded. When the ordeal ended, the great ghosts and the beasts suddenly vanished entirely.
Zhili turned back to look, but not a single thing was to be seen; he then leaped over a wall and fled southward, not knowing where he was going.
It felt as though in the space of a single bound he had traveled a thousand li. Again, he saw a ghost pursuing him and covering him with an iron cage.
As he did so, countless fish vied with one another to come and devour them. After a long while, the ghost returned, but the fish were nowhere to be seen.
A monk whom his family had previously supported had died some time ago; he appeared and helped Zhili remove the cage, saying to him:
Dānapati was suffering from a great famine. [The monk] gave him three white pills, the size of jujubes, and told him to bow and eat them.

At that moment, he became fully satiated. Then [the monk] said to him, "Dānapati, return home; I, the monk, shall also depart. As Dānapati bowed and reached the north of his residence, he saw a large pit.
Within it were various spears and lances planted in a dense thicket, making it impossible to pass through. There he saw his elder brother’s daughter along with a maidservant.
He carried a chest, along with money, silk, and a vessel of food and drink, located to the northeast of the pit.
Zhili took this maidservant and his niece in his heart to play with them; he found this very strange. Turning his head to look north, he immediately saw a ghost.
Brandishing his sword, he charged straight forward. Zhili, struck with terror, threw herself into a pit and immediately regained consciousness.
From her initial death until her rebirth, six days had passed in total. Later, when she questioned her family, she learned that it was her niece who had carried paper money and silk [to the funeral].
Upon opening and examining what had been sent, he saw only copper coins, silk, and brocade.

During the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, when the army campaigned against Kucha, there was a man named Sagun who served as the Assistant Director of the Granary Office for the expeditionary force.
After the city of Kucha was captured, he subsequently stripped the face of a Buddha statue in a monastery to take the gold; within ten days—
His eyebrows fell out entirely. He returned to Yizhou, where he repented before the Buddha and dedicated all the gold he had acquired toward the creation of meritorious works.
Before long, his eyebrows grew back again.
In the household of Lu Huaisu of Wu Commandery during the Tang dynasty, a fire broke out in the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era, and all the buildings were completely consumed by the flames.
Even the meditation hall was reduced to ashes; yet, a single case containing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* remained alone.

Both the case and the silk binding were entirely destroyed, but the characters of the scripture themselves were not burned at all. At that time, among those who heard of this, there were none who did not [marvel].
He did not express any surprise. Huaisu was the elder brother of Xu Renze’s former wife;
Renze had witnessed it with his own eyes and later recounted the account in full.
Yang Shicao was a native of Dongyang Township in Liquan County, Yongzhou during the Tang dynasty.
At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, he served as the Director of the Bamboo Park (Sizhu Jian). Later, due to official business, he was transferred to the post of Magistrate of Lantian County.

In the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era, because of his advanced age, he returned home and took up farming as his livelihood. However, Shicao was by nature malicious and foul-mouthed; throughout his life, he had been prone to...
He observed the transgressions of others; whenever a person of the district had a matter, he would record it and report it to the authorities.
Because the County Office treated him with deference—since Cao had previously served in court and held official rank—he harbored long-standing malice and refused to reform.

He repeatedly harassed the offices of government, seeking out matters involving his fellow villagers regardless of their magnitude, constantly instilling fear and intimidation. Within his own village community, he would arbitrarily create disturbances where none existed and impose his own arbitrary regulations.
People of all ranks engaged in idle disputes over right and wrong, while cattle and sheep trampled the paths and men and women vied with one another.

They would immediately take their grievances to the county office. The Magistrate Pei Gautama initially adjudicated two or three cases, but later, seeing the increasing volume of affairs, he ceased to provide justice.
Cao subsequently traveled through the prefecture, sometimes submitting petitions that reached the imperial court; however, his malicious intent grew daily, and no one [could restrain him].
Xijian Cao was aware that his own nature was wicked; he also told others, "My disposition is prone to impetuosity and violence.
Since the Wude era, he had received the precepts four times, maintained his practice and performed prostrations, recited sutras and treatises daily, and exhorted others toward goodness.
However, whenever anyone, great or small, encroached upon him, he could not bear it. Later, on the night of the seventh day of the fourth month in the first year of the Yonghui era, he...
Suddenly, a man came from the east, riding a white horse and wearing a green robe. He went straight to Cao’s gate. Upon seeing him, Cao greeted him with the customary pleasantries.
The man said, "The Great Inspector of Dongyang has specifically sent me to pursue you.

Since your birth, you have been bound by a poisonous heart that he cannot bear to abandon. Whenever he encounters someone, he speaks to them, urging them toward goodness; yet he himself does not observe the precepts."

[The Buddha] said, "He was entirely stingy and greedy, refusing to give. He claimed, 'I possess a virtuous mind and shall make offerings to the Triple Gem,' yet he never gave so much as a single coin.
Though his mouth spoke of shame and remorse, in his heart he immediately conceived perverse schemes that deluded ordinary people.
For this reason, I summoned you; yet for a moment, no one came to him. As he stood at the gate, he suddenly fell to the ground, unable to speak, [only]..."

His heart felt a slight warmth. His family members carried him on a litter back to his house, where he lay down; however, after one night had passed, he did not revive. Yet Cao had already arrived at the Dongyang Dulu office.
At that time, the Magistrate’s grand court session had not yet dispersed. Cao then went privately through the various bureaus;

they all possessed desks, writing tablets, beds, and mats, which were exceedingly large, exquisite, and fine. There were also prisoners there, some wearing shackles and chains, with their heads bared and their waists untied.
Whether sitting, standing, walking, or staying—such sinners were beyond counting. Cao proceeded eastward until he reached a certain place where the openings were extremely small;
from them, sparks of fire flowed out along with foul-smelling smoke and flames that could not even accommodate a person standing upright.
Furthermore, there were two men holding iron clubs, guarding the entrance. Cao asked the men holding the clubs, "What is this place?"
The official replied, "This is the Hell of Fierce Fire. It is intended for those who were incomplete in their observance of the precepts, or those who ceased their cultivation of goodness mid-course;

those who, knowing full well, committed offenses intentionally, shall upon death enter this place. We have heard that there was once a Master Yang Sicao who delighted his entire life in discussing the faults of others.
He would constantly inform the authorities of their long and short comings, yet whenever he encountered anyone, he would feign remorse. He possessed even a fragment of..."

[The character for "凌" (líng) is missing; it should read 凌 (líng)]. Indeed, he could not endure [the hardship]. Now, wishing to send him into this place, I have repaired [the path]. Today is the eighth day of the fourth month.
His family, on account of his death, has prepared offerings for a vegetarian feast.

The officials have deliberated and wish to release him back home, yet they have not yet received instructions. I am here waiting for Master Cáo. Cáo then prostrated himself with his head to the ground in gratitude and withdrew.
He said, "The disciple Yang Sicao is that very person. I pray you will employ skillful means so that he may attain liberation.

The man replied, "If you simply pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions with a sincere heart and repent with earnest devotion, turning back your poisonous mind, you will immediately follow me to be reborn there and not return to this place.
Although you harbored evil intent, if you can repent for the duration of one life, it is like the practice of a Bodhisattva; do not spare your own body."
He was granted life and attained rebirth in the Pure Land. After Master Cáo received these words, he immediately followed the instructions to confess his transgressions with earnest sincerity.
Consequently, [the patient] was released and returned home, where he recovered after three days. Once Cáo had regained consciousness, he recounted this matter in full detail.
Later, Cáo went to the place of Meditation Master Huìjìng to repent for his past errors; he remains alive today at the age of seventy.

He was fifteen years old. Every time he ate, he would observe a strict fast for six periods of the day, performing prostrations and repentance. While working in the fields on the official road, he went out to inspect the wheat;
he saw three oxen greedily devouring the wheat seedlings. Cao approached the oxen with a sense of shame and did not drive them away.

After returning home, when he went to the field the following day, the wheat had not died, but there were only the tracks of the oxen. To the west of Jingyang, within its borders, was the Buddhist hall of King Chen, which was extensive.
People gathered together. Cao recounted the matter to the assembly. Both monastics and laypeople were struck with wonder, and their devotional repentance became even more earnest.
That night, he dreamed of someone coming to speak to him, saying: "I am a messenger sent specifically to admonish you.

Since you have ceased your evil ways, we shall no longer pursue you. Provided that you remain diligent and sincere in cultivating goodness, there is no need for concern. A monk who saw Cao [reported this].
This was related by Xianglin.
In Dunqiu County of Jizhou during the Tang dynasty, there was an elderly woman surnamed Li, approximately seventy years of age. Childless and living in solitude, she had only two servants.
Her household business consisted of selling wine; she would add ash to the liquor and measure it out with extreme precision, down to the smallest fraction. This was during the Zhenguan era.
In the midst of this, his vital breath was severed by illness. He had been dead for two days, and the funeral implements were already prepared;
however, because there was a slight warmth remaining in his heart, he subsequently revived. He said: "At first, there were two men both dressed in red garments who summoned me out at the gate.
There was an official edict ordering my pursuit, so I immediately followed them. We traveled until we reached a city that resembled a provincial seat. They led me into a side courtyard, where I saw—"

An official sat at his desk, dressed in a large-sleeved robe and formal cap, with many attendants on either side. Beneath the steps were numerous people wearing shackles and collars, guarded as if they were living beings.
The magistrate sent someone to question the old woman: "For what reason do you sell wine so recklessly and take so much from others?
You have intended to copy the Lotus Sūtra for nearly ten years; why have you not yet produced it? The old woman explained in detail: [...the rest of the text follows...]

He said, "The wine was made by a maidservant; the measure was also [made by] a maidservant. Having finished the recitation, he gave one thousand coins to Master Yin and immediately dispatched someone to pursue the maidservant.
She arrived in a short while. Upon investigating the original circumstances, the maidservant was flogged forty times and then released to return home.
He sent someone to ask Master Yin, who replied, "It is true. He then said to the old woman, "I release you for seven days to go; once the recitation is finished, you must come back."
She was reborn in a favorable realm and subsequently regained her life. Furthermore, someone asked about the old woman’s death and had it investigated.

It was found that when she first died, the maidservant had regained consciousness after a long time before reviving; her abdomen and back were swollen and bluish, which were clearly the marks of forty lash wounds.
Master Yin was originally a visiting monk assigned to Dunqiu Temple; he was nearly sixty or seventy years old, and since his ordination...

He practiced the dhūta of begging for food and always observed the single-meal fast, never ceasing even for a moment. Virtuous monks from both near and far all held him in deep respect and admiration.
After his elderly mother passed away, Master Yin dreamed that a man dressed in red came to question him; in the dream, he replied, "The production of this scripture is indeed true.
Thereupon, his mother requested the local kin and relatives, as well as Master Yin the Chan master, to perform rites for her, and they hired various scribes to transcribe the scriptures.

Shengzhong transcribed the sutra by hand. When the transcription was completed, exactly seven days later, he again saw the two men from before come forward. His mother said, "The messenger has arrived;
they are all dwelling well. As soon as these words ended, she died. Master Yin remained alive. He was held in reverence by both monastics and laypeople.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a man serving as the magistrate of a county in Suizhou who traveled to Gaochang. There, he obtained a statue made of pearls from a temple.
Upon arriving at the capital, he wished to purchase it from various major temples for a thousand strings of cash, but they refused to sell it; he subsequently destroyed it.
He sold it for one thousand three hundred *kuan*. Over a month later, he suffered from a swelling.
During his sleep, he saw a monk who said, "For what reason did you destroy a sacred image? The monk then sent someone to pull out his tongue, which was over a foot long.
He groaned in agony and died after several days. Xue Da, the Magistrate of De'an County, was fully aware of these events.
In the third year of the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty, while Xu Yu was serving as the Prefect of Jinzhou, there was a butcher in the eastern alley of the market who slaughtered a pig.

When the life was severed and it was placed in boiling water to be scalded, the skin and hair fell off entirely. Although it had been dead for half a day, he remained greedy and went on to slaughter more pigs.

Before he had time to open his eyes and understand what was happening, dawn arrived; he slit open his belly with a knife. He made a long incision across his abdomen, yet even after the first blade had been drawn, it had not yet fully entered his belly.
Suddenly, the pig rose up and ran out the door, heading straight for the western wall of the marketplace. It went to the shop of a certain worthy man and lay down beneath his bed.
The people of the market vied with one another to go and see it, while the butcher still pursued it with his knife in hand. Those who were watching asked him:
The butcher replied, "In all my life, I have never heard of or seen such a thing while slaughtering pigs.
He still wished to take it away, but several hundred onlookers, all indignant at the butcher, vied with one another to pay money to redeem it.
The people collectively built a shed to house it; only after a long time did its body hair grow back, and the sores beneath its throat and belly healed.
He had developed a large fleshy tumor as thick as an arm; yet, whether entering or exiting, coming or going, he never soiled his dwelling.
His nature was pure and unlike that of other pigs. He died at the age of four or five (as related by Wang Tongren, a native of Jinyang County in Bingzhou and a clerk in the Xu Prince’s household).
The monk Yifu was a native of Qingshe. He was skilled at playing the *qin* lute and resided at Longxing Temple in Jiangling.
His conduct was eccentric and unconventional, yet the provincial governor tolerated him and provided him with money and silk to travel to Western Sichuan to copy the Tripitaka.
When someone stole a set of the Tripitaka commissioned by a lay devotee and put it up for sale, Yifu redeemed it for a low price; he then used the surplus funds for his own purposes.
There was one who once discovered that a seller of scriptures had died beneath a withered tree. Although this monk escaped punishment, he soon fell ill;
his two lips turned upward as if they were the mouth of a donkey, and he suffered from a burning pain so unbearable that no one dared to look upon him.
Having endured every form of agony, he died. Several others in the same monastery who had been trafficking in scriptures and images became fearful and relinquished their wealth.
Cultivating Merit with Faith as a Mirror and Caution.
*Mingbao ji jishu*, Scroll Four.
*Mingbao ji jishu*, Scroll Five.
During the Zhenguan era, Li Yiyen of Longxi in the Tang dynasty served as the County尉 (magistrate) of Hua Prefecture.

Suddenly, one person went missing from this county, and his whereabouts remained unknown. His father and elder brother suspected that he had been murdered by an enemy or a vengeful relative, so they went to the county office to present their plea.

Yiyen investigated the case but could not reach a definitive conclusion. In the middle of the night, he took up a candle and interrogated them with meticulous detail. By the second watch of the night, Yiyen—
Leaning over his desk with his head bowed, he was unaware that the dead man had already arrived, still bearing the marks of his injuries. He said, "I, [Name], have been wounded;
I was beaten to death and placed in a well at such-and-such a location. You may search for me soon, otherwise I fear I will be moved elsewhere and cannot be found.
Yiyen immediately went there in person to search, and it was exactly as described. Shortly thereafter, the avenger...
The family said, "We have just begun our prostrations. Those who heard and saw this at the time could not help but be struck with wonder and admiration.
Previously, at Qingchan Temple in the Western Capital of the Tang, there was a statue made of pure gold, one foot four inches in height and weighing eighty *liang*.
It had been commissioned by Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty. In the fourteenth year of the Zhenguan era, there was a thief named Sun Dexin who feigned—

He forged an imperial edict and sent a eunuch boy, falsely claiming he had been dispatched by the Emperor to take the image. When the temple monks heard that they had been summoned by imperial decree, they dared not refuse and handed it over to him.
After one night, the matter was discovered; the body of the image had already been melted down and broken apart, though the head alone remained unmelted.
Emperor Taizong was greatly incensed and sentenced him to the ultimate punishment. Before De-xin died, his body had already rotted away, with sores covering his entire frame.
The mold broke. The temple monks added more gold and recast it according to the proper rites.
Li Siyi of Longxi, who lived during the Tang dynasty and now resides in Fuyang County of Xiangzhou, died on the first day of the first month in the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era;

he revived after one day. The account of his speech is recorded in the *Mingbao ji* (Records of Miraculous Retribution). Furthermore, in the fifth month of the third year of the Yonghui era, [he again...]
He died and revived after one night. He recounted that, as his life span was not yet exhausted, he had been granted permission by the King to return home.

Before the King, he saw the monk Bian-gui of Fa-guan Monastery in Fu-yang County, Xiangzhou; he also saw the monks Hong-liang and Hui-bao of Hui-fu Monastery—these three were all present before the King.
Bian responded to the question of whether he had seen the underworld officials, saying, "Hui-bao’s time for death has not yet come."
"It would be most appropriate to cultivate meritorious deeds. Bian Gui and Hongliang will surely die this year. That year, Bian Gui and the others indeed passed away one after another.
Later, the monks of the monastery sent a medium to the former quarters of Hongliang and the others to summon two monks and question them.
Bian Gui said, "Because I broke my fast, I am now undergoing great suffering. He further told his disciples, "Perform a vegetarian feast on my behalf to rescue me from this hardship.
The disciples immediately prepared the feast. The shaman then declared, "Bian Gui has already been absolved of his offense.
Hong Liang said, "I broke my fast and furthermore slandered others; I am now being punished by having my tongue pulled out."
It is painful; one cannot speak of it further. This was related by the monk Huiyong and others of Zhili Temple in Xiangzhou.
Shi Zhikai, a native of Lihu in Caozhou during the Tang dynasty, had been fond of the Buddhist scriptures since his youth and did not serve in government office.

He remained unmarried, donned monastic robes, and lived in seclusion on Mount Tai, making the recitation of sutras his primary practice. In the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era, while in the mountains...
Encountering an illness that brought him to the brink of death, he covered his body with his *kāṣāya* robe and fell into a state of profound unconsciousness like a dream.
He saw an old woman and several dozen beautiful women repeatedly coming to disturb him. Zhikai remained upright and unmoving; the group of women gradually pressed closer and rebuked him, all saying:
The sedan chair was about to be thrown into the northern ravine. Thereupon, they all moved forward together and simultaneously seized hold of it; some grabbed onto his *kāṣāya*.

They then chanted the Buddha’s name in unison, followed by repentance and a request that he be made into an Amitābha Buddha, while also reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva more than thirty times.
After a short while, they felt great perspiration break out over their bodies, and he immediately recovered.
Qi Shiwang, a native of Wuchang in Wei Prefecture during the Tang dynasty, died in the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era. After seven days, he revived and related his own account:
"After I first died, I was led before the King and immediately handed over to the judicial officials for a separate investigation.

After four or five days, the examination of the registers revealed that my name was identical to that of someone due to die at that time; thus, it was not yet appropriate for me to die. The judicial official..."
He said to Shi Wang, "In your lifetime you were fond of roasting chicken eggs; you ought to go back and undergo your retribution.
He immediately ordered someone to escort him out the gate. After traveling one or two *li* from the office, Shi Wang saw a city.
Hearing the sound of drums and music within the city, he joyfully hurried toward it and entered. Once he had entered, the city gates were already closed, and further inside...
There were no houses; the entire ground was covered with hot ashes. Śiṅgāla was distraught and did not know what to do. His feet were scorched, causing him extraordinary agony.
Śiṅgāla looked around and saw that the city gates were all open. As he rushed toward a gate, its doors closed behind him. This continued for an entire day.
Then someone commanded the gatekeeper, saying, "Open the gate and release the criminal of yesterday. Once [the gate was opened]...
He emerged and immediately ordered his attendants to escort him back. The messengers excused themselves, citing the great distance of the road, and delayed their departure.
They then began to demand money and silk; Shi Wang consented, and so they traveled across rivers and roads, treading through thorns and brambles.
Upon reaching a certain place, there was a space like a small enclosure, within which lay a deep, black pit. Shi Wang was terrified by it, but the messenger pushed him, and he fell into the pit.
Inside, he gradually regained consciousness without realizing it. He immediately prepared paper money and waited for him.
When the messenger arrived at the appointed time, Shi Wang and his wife saw him together.
Liu Shanjing, a native of Xicheng in Fenzhou during the Tang dynasty, was orphaned at a young age and raised by his mother.
Throughout her life, his mother had regularly studied the Buddhist scriptures and practiced asceticism with diligent devotion. She passed away in the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era.

Shanjing mourned her with such profound grief that he observed the prescribed rites of mourning, his wailing never ceasing. In the following year, while Shanjing was in a state of dazed reverie, he saw his mother and she said to him:
"I cultivated merit during my previous life and thus received a male body. I am now born here in the Song family at Shizhao Village, south of this county.
If you wish to see me, you may go there immediately. Having spoken these words, he vanished. Following his instructions, Shanjing went there and arrived before long.
On that very day, a son was born to the Song family. Consequently, Shanjing presented them with clothing and offerings.
The account is based on these details. This man is still living. Shanjing has always served him with the etiquette due to a mother.
The śramaṇa Shanfu of Xizhou was an old acquaintance of Shanjing; having heard what Shanjing and his fellow villagers said, he related it for the sake of others.
During the late Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, Lu Yuanli of Fanyang served as the Magistrate of Lianhui County in Sizhou.
Once, having fallen into a deep stupor from a severe illness, he revived after one day and said: "Someone led me to an official residence, where I saw an official pass by without any attendants.
I then proceeded to the seat of this official and sat upon the couch. The official signaled to his attendant."
He ordered one hand to seize Yuanli’s head and the other to grasp his feet, then threw him down onto the steps below. After a long while, Yuanli rose;
he walked to a separate courtyard and proceeded further south into a large hall.
There he saw several hundred cooking cauldrons, from which steam rose straight up like clouds and mist, the sound of the boiling clamorous and chaotic as if there were tens of millions of people.
Ren Yuanli looked up and saw what appeared to be a person contained within a cage, suspended above this vapor. It was said to be the place where sinful people were steamed.
Yuanli then made a vow and spoke aloud, saying, "I shall undergo this suffering on behalf of all sentient beings.
He immediately removed his clothes, stood naked, and threw himself into the cauldron; consequently, he instantly became unconscious and felt no pain. After a short while, there was a śramaṇa...
The gatekeeper pulled Yuanli out and said, "I know your utmost sincerity," and then sent him back home. Suddenly, as if waking from a dream, he ceased consuming alcohol and meat.
After three or four years had passed, he died in Luoyang.
The monk Xuangao of Zhili Temple in Fuyang County, Xiangzhou, was surnamed Zhao. His nephew had previously been born as a son in the Ma family of the same village.

When this boy of the Ma family died at the end of the Zhenguan era, on his deathbed he looked toward his mother and said, "I have a karmic connection from a previous life with the Zhao clan; after I die, I shall become a grandson to that clan."
Zong was from the same village as her. Her mother did not believe it, so she marked the boy’s left flank with ink to create a large black mole.
Later, Zhao’s wife had a dream in which this child came to her and said, "I shall be your son. Consequently, she became pregnant;
the child seen in the dream was exactly like the one from the Ma family. After the birth, it was verified that the ink mark was still there on the original spot.
As for the location: when the boy was three years old, there being no one to guide him, he went by himself to the Ma family’s house and said, "This is my former residence;
it still exists today, and I am already fourteen or fifteen years old. This was related by the monks Huiling and Fazhen of Zhili Temple in Xiangzhou.
Pei Zeman, a native of Li xu in Caozhou during the Tang dynasty, died at the age of twenty-one at the end of the Zhenguan era.
After three days, he revived and recounted that when he first died, he was led by a man to the presence of the King. The King wore white robes that were exceptionally bright and clean.
The King sent this man to plow the fields with oxen. The man petitioned, saying, "My brothers are young and there is no one to care for our two parents.
The King took pity on him and dispatched a messenger to lead him southward. Upon reaching the third gate, he entered and saw cauldrons of boiling water, mountains of blades, and forests of swords.
He further saw the heads of several thousand people, all severed and spread out upon the ground. This...
Both the head and the mouth cried out, "I am starving. In that village there was an old woman, nearly seventy years of age, who had not yet died;
she was seen tending the fire before the cauldron of boiling water. After observing this, he returned to the presence of the King and saw his fellow villager Zhang Cheng, who was also not yet dead.
Someone accused Cheng, saying, "He destroyed my house. The King dispatched an envoy to investigate him.
He replied, "This is true. Cheng said, "I was not aware that the ground was a burial mound; I broke open the tomb unintentionally.
The King said, "Though you acted unintentionally, your mind was ultimately lacking in care. He then ordered someone to strike him seven times on the waist with a staff.
After a short while, the king said, "You have no further business here; release you so that you may return early. The king then dispatched men to escort him away.

As he went out through the north gate, he climbed over a wall and, looking down from atop it, saw his house. He then heard the sound of weeping and leaped down from the wall. Suddenly, he found himself sitting up.
After he had regained consciousness, he related everything in detail to the people of his village. When the villagers looked at Zhang Cheng’s waist, they saw—
Seventh, the mark left by the fallen staff was an intense dark blue-black. When asked about the desecration of the tomb, he replied that it was not false.
The old mother soon fell ill and died before long.
At Shibi Temple in Bingzhou during the Tang dynasty, there was an elderly monk whose vocation was the practice of meditation and recitation. He was diligent and refined in his conduct.
Toward the end of the Zhenguan era, a dove nested upon a pillar in his room and raised two fledglings. Whenever the Dharma Master had leftover food, he would regularly go to the nest to feed them.
Although the dove chicks gradually grew larger afterward, their wings were not yet fully formed; thus, when they attempted to fly together, they both fell to the ground.
The two died, and the monks buried them together. Ten days later, the monks dreamed at night that two young boys said to them:
"We previously committed minor offenses and consequently received the bodies of pigeons. Recently, we heard the Dharma Master reciting the Lotus Sūtra and the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra;
having heard this sublime Dharma, we have now attained human bodies. We are currently by the side of this temple..."
More than ten *li* away, at a certain village, a man named [Name] was to receive a rebirth as a male child. Beyond ten months, he was due to be born.
The monk went to visit that household according to the appointed time and saw that a woman had given birth to two sons simultaneously;
they were then performing a *pūrṇamāsa* (month-filling) feast. The monk called out, "Pigeon! and both children responded in unison, saying, "Yes. One of them responded.

More than a year later, she finally spoke [of her experience]. (This one account follows in the *Mingbao Shiyi*). The details of the matter of repaying kindness are too extensive to be related in full.
There was a woman surnamed Zhu from Yangwu County in Zhengzhou during the Tang dynasty; her husband had previously owed a person from a neighboring county one hundred bolts of silk.
After her husband died, no one ever returned from there. Toward the end of the Zhenguan era, she fell ill and died; after two nights had passed, she revived.
She said that people had seized her and brought her to a certain place, where she saw a man who said, "I am an official of the Office of Destiny (Siming Fu).
Your husband owed my house several bolts of silk during his lifetime; that is why we pursued you. We now release you to return home; you must quickly prepare the goods."
"Go to such-and-such a village in such-and-such a county and return my mother to me. If she is not returned, I shall send men to seize her with even greater urgency.
Furthermore, speak on my behalf to my mother and urge her to strive to create an image of me and cultivate merit for my sake.

Zhu then made his request, and the villagers obtained silk to return to his mother, describing in detail the appearance of her son, noting that it was identical to how he had been when alive. His mother, in turn, wept before him.
He wept and sobbed for a long time.
*Mingbao ji jishu*, Fascicle Five;
*Mingbao ji jishu*, Fascicle Six.
During the Yonghui era, Lu Bodai, a native of Xiaoyi County in Fenzhou during the Tang dynasty, owed one thousand coins to a man from the same county.

Later, he breached their agreement and refused to acknowledge the debt. When the creditor presented the contract to demand repayment, Lu Bodai went before a Buddha statue with his creditor and made a solemn oath, saying:
"If I do not repay you, I vow that after my death, I shall become a beast of burden for your household."
Having finished speaking, he died before a year had passed. When his second year arrived, a cow belonging to the owner of the money gave birth to a red calf at the house of the creditor;
on its forehead grew white hair forming the three characters "Lu Bo Da. His sons and nephews were ashamed of this.

He offered five thousand coins to redeem [the image], but the owner refused to give it up. He then bestowed it upon the monk Zhenru of Qifu Temple in Xicheng County to assist in the construction of a fifteen-story pagoda.
Those who saw this were moved to resolve their minds toward goodness and refrain from evil, vying with one another to offer money and goods as alms.
During the Yonghui era, Wei Zhishi of Jingzhao, a military official in the Right Golden Myriarchy, boiled the leg of a sheep; it remained half-cooked even after half a day.
Enraged, Zhishi told his family members, "I am using ten times as much firewood as usual, yet I do not know why it has turned out like this.
He ordered it to be boiled again, but it returned to its former state. He then ordered it to be cut open, and inside he discovered a bronze image.
It was over one cun in length; its radiance was brilliant and its marks and signs were fully perfected. From that time on, the family never again dared to consume wine or meat.
Lang Yuling of Zhongshan personally heard this account.
Wang Huai-zhi, a native of Fangzhou during the Tang dynasty and a Grand Pillar of State (Shangzhuguo), passed away at the beginning of the Xianqing era.
His mother, Lady Sun, as well as his younger brothers Huai-shan and Huai-biao, all survived. In the sixth month of the fourth year [of Xianqing], there was a man in Gaoling, Yongzhou.
His name and surname have been lost. Seven days after his death, his back had already begun to rot when he revived.
Beneath the earth, this man saw Huai-zhi, who said, "I am currently serving as the Registrar of Taishan. I have sent this man to take up the brush, and I dictate this letter for him.
He then said to him, "Although you were destined to die, I have now used skillful means to release you to return home. You should carry this letter to my residence for me."
The Prefect visited my home and informed my mother that Huai-zhi was currently serving as the Clerk of Records for Mount Tai;

he was fortunately at peace and well. However, our family had previously borrowed timber from the monastery to construct a gate. Since this was property dedicated to religious merit, I request that it be repaid promptly.
Huai-shan has already died and should not remain here any longer; please quickly commission scriptures and images to assist him, otherwise—
I feared there was no way to save him. After this man had revived, he immediately took the letter and delivered it to his former residence;
the matters discussed therein accorded with reality in every detail. When three days had passed, Huai-shan suddenly died.

Among the monastics and laypeople who heard of this throughout the entire prefecture, there were none who did not increase their cultivation of merit. This was related by Zhi-chun, the Commandery Guard of Xunzhou.
Xie Houjun was a native of Fucheng in Jizhou. In the second year of the Xianqing era, he fell ill and remained in a state of delirium for over forty days, nearly dying.
He spoke of himself, saying: "I have been conscripted as an ox and have frequently undergone bitter suffering. I appeal to you:

I once received the precepts and performed repentance three times before Master Yin; I examined myself and found no transgressions. How can you bear to make me an ox and subject my body to such misery?"
It was so. He had already been assigned to a mill for twenty days. After being subjected to harsh labor, he was subsequently examined and found fit to receive the precepts;
this was indeed true and not false, and only then was he released from punishment. Throughout his life, this man possessed great physical strength; he was a heavy drinker and fond of fighting.
Now, however, he has completely abandoned alcohol and meat and is a pure-faith lay devotee, observing the fasts and precepts without ceasing as a disciple of Master Yin.
In the northern market of the Western Market in the Tang capital of Chang’an, there was a man named Wang Huishi whose mother had passed away.
Once his period of mourning had concluded, in the second year of the Xianqing era, a yellowish-green female dog was born in his household.
Huishi’s wife, suspecting the dog of stealing food, struck it several times with a staff. The dog then spoke in human speech, saying: "I am your paternal aunt. New...
"The wife said, 'I have committed a great error in striking you. I was excessively harsh toward my family members, and thus I have received this retribution.

Now that I have been beaten, I am ashamed to face your household,' whereupon she immediately fled. When Master Hui heard of this, he wept with grief and tried to detain her to bring her home, but she departed once more.
This happened four or five times in total. Seeing that her resolve was firm, Master Hui finally yielded and invited her to the main street north of the market."
This was precisely the north wall of his own shop. Later, he built a small shed there to house it and sent food to it every day.
The number of market people and travelers who came to visit it was extremely great; those who threw cakes to it were beyond counting.
This dog never left the shed; once the mealtime had passed, it refused to eat. After one or two years, no one knew where it had gone.
Liu Mo’er, a native of Xianquan Village in Xiaoyi County, Fenzhou, under the Tang dynasty, passed away on the twenty-seventh day of the eighth month in the fourth year of the Xianqing era.
His son, Shi Bao, died the following day. Throughout their lives, the conduct of both father and son had been treacherous and perverse.
A neighbor to their north, Qi Longwei, was killed by being run over by a cart while gathering firewood. After several...
He revived at sunrise and saw that his son Ma'er and his tutor were within a cauldron of boiling water. In a mere moment, their skin and flesh were completely consumed;
they no longer had human form, but were seen only as white bones. After this state had persisted for a long while, they returned to their original forms.
Longwei asked them the reason for this, and they replied, "We have suffered this retribution because we hunted for him. He then asked the tutor, "What about your father?"
He replied, "My father’s transgressions are grave; he cannot be seen immediately. Once you have returned, I beg that you inform my family so that they may perform a vegetarian feast for his merit.
Having finished speaking, he was urged on by the messenger and proceeded to the government office.

There he saw the buildings were lofty and imposing, and more than twenty men stood guard with weapons. An official asked him, "What meritorious deeds have you performed recently? He replied, "In Long..."
Last year in the first month, Wei was reading the *Sarvadharmaparyāya* at Duku Village.
He offered a robe as a gift and simultaneously received the five precepts, which he has not violated until now. The official said, "If it is as you say, his merit is immeasurable;

why then has he come here? He then requested the register to verify it. Upon examining the register, it was seen that the man was indeed destined for death, and there was a marginal note stating: "Received [the precepts]."
The merit of the precepts and the gift of alms combined to further extend his life, so that he was sent back by messenger and immediately revived.
Zhou [surname only], whose given name is forgotten, served as the County Assistant Magistrate of Guantao in Jizhou during the Tang dynasty.

In the eleventh month of the fourth year of the Xianqing era, he was dispatched on an official mission to the Linyu Pass for trade. At the time of his departure, he was accompanied by two subordinates and clerks.
As time passed, Zhou’s money and silk gradually increased in amount. The two men then used an earthen sack to crush him to death and stole all his money and silk;
they took only the clothes he was wearing for the funeral.

At the end of the year, Zhou entered his wife's dream and described in detail how he had been killed, as well as stating the locations where the stolen goods were hidden. His wife then acted accordingly.

This was reported to the authorities. The judicial officials investigated the case and obtained the full facts; both men were apprehended with the money and silk, and they were all sentenced to death.
The monk Huiyong of Zhili Temple in Xiangzhou stated that he personally witnessed this when the Daoist Liu Renshi recounted it to him in the Hall of Brightness (Mingtang).
Li Qian-guan of Longxi in the Tang dynasty currently resides in Zhengzhou.

In the fifth year of the Xianqing era, while observing the mourning period for his father, he drew blood to transcribe one scroll each of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Prajñāhṛdaya Sūtra*, and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Just as he was about to go outside with them, he bathed his body. Subsequently, a most extraordinary fragrance suddenly wafted from within the courtyard.
Its fragrance was so intense that it permeated the surrounding area; everyone who went to view it offered words of praise.
Zhongshan Lang Yuling once passed through Zhengzhou and spoke of this in detail to his friends there.
Xindu Yuanfang was a native of Fuyang County in Xiangzhou during the Tang dynasty. From his youth, he possessed noble character and was particularly devoted to the Buddhist scriptures.
At the age of twenty-nine, in the first month of spring in the fifth year of the Xianqing era, he died.

More than a month after his death, his elder brother Daonie, a monk at Faguang Temple, feeling a deep sense of fraternal affection, summoned a female shaman to his home and dispatched her to seek Yuanfang.
Yu Faguang was also somewhat proficient in magical arts. He then produced a talisman to capture Yuan Fang and ordered a shaman to question him regarding the details of his situation.
The shaman could not read characters, so he sent for a scribe to take dictation; the shaman orally dictated to Yuan Fang as he composed a letter on one sheet of paper.
He gave it to his fellow student Feng Xingji, in which he fully set forth the intent of his entire life, along with two poems.
He also left a letter for his family. Its composition was orderly and its words were sorrowful.

The general purport of the letter exhorted them to cultivate merit, specifically by practicing mindfulness of the Buddha and transcribing sutras, stating that among all karmic offenses, none is greater than the act of killing.
It further stated: "Yuanfang shall not enter hell, nor shall he fall among the hungry ghosts. Previously...
She was assigned by the officials of the Mōngmíng bureau to become a son in the household of Lǐ Rénshī in Shízhōu;
however, because Shí Míngyuǎn of Wúshān County in Lǒngzhōu had prayed for a son at Huáyè Peak, she was instead transferred to the Shí family to be their son.
It is further said that the date of her birth was imminent and she could no longer remain [in the womb]; from the second month she was conceived, and in the twelfth month she was born.
"I pray that you, my elder brothers, will extend your compassion and go there to see him. Having spoken these words, he departed with tears streaming down his face.
Xue Dazao of Hedong was residing in Fuyang; he had previously served as the Magistrate of Wushan County and stated that he personally knew Renyuan.
This was related by the monks Huiyong and Fazhen of Zili Temple.
Tang Fengyuanze was a native of Changhe in Bohai. During the Xianqing era, he served as the Chief Cook for the Imperial Kitchen at the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
At that time, the King of Khotan from the Western Regions came to court; there were several hundred sheep remaining from the provisions for his meal.
The King entrusted Yuanze with sending them all to Buddhist monasteries to be released as "eternal life" (longsheng). Yuanze then secretly ordered—

A butcher was slaughtering livestock and collecting the payment when, on the sixth day of the summer month in the first year of the Longshuo era, a great rain fell upon Luoyang accompanied by thunder and a lightning strike that struck Yuanze.
He was killed in the middle of the main street outside Xuanren Gate; his neck was broken and blood gushed forth, drenching the ground.
Spectators filled the streets, all of whom were struck with astonishment.

The layman Li Xin of the Tang dynasty was a native of Taiping Village in Wen-shui County of Bingzhou. He served as a *long* (high official).
I was a government guard. In the winter of the Xianqing era, I followed the regulations to Shuo Prefecture to serve my term. I rode a chestnut grass-fed horse and brought along a foal.
At that time, as the year drew to a close, the sky was overcast and the wind and snow were bitter and thick.

After traveling ten or so li, the horse suddenly stopped moving forward. Fearing that the deadline for my term was imminent, I struck it several dozen times with my whip. The horse then spoke in human speech.
Śraddhā said, "I am your mother. Because I avoided your father during my lifetime and went begging for a handful of rice for you, I have received this retribution.
This colt is your sister; she has already repaid her debt with her labor. Why do you still press me so hard with such grief?
Upon hearing this, Śraddhā was struck with astonishment and wept, unable to control herself; she then bowed in gratitude and personally...

Xìn took the pack-saddle and bridle and said, "If you are truly my sister, you should return home by yourself. The horse then proceeded forward, and Xìn, carrying the saddle and bridle, followed it until they reached home.
When Xìn’s brothers saw this, they wept in sorrow as they faced one another. They separately prepared a stable and manger to provide fodder for the horse, while Xìn remained with his mother.
They invited monks to perform a vegetarian feast, and throughout the entire family, everyone practiced with diligent devotion. The same was true among the laypeople and clergy of the local community.

Everyone sighed in admiration of this marvel. At that time, Wen Wuyin, Vice Minister of Works, and Zhang Jinting, Judicial Official of Qizhou, were both observing the mourning period for their parents;

hearing of this, they found it extraordinary and went to visit the Xins’ residence. They saw that the horse was still there and inquired about the circumstances, and everything was exactly as had been reported.
During the Xianqing era, there was a man from Pingzhou named Sun Shou who was hunting along the seashore.
He saw a wild fire blazing so fiercely that the grasses and trees were completely consumed, yet only one thicket of lush vegetation remained unburnt.
Suspecting there might be a beast within this grass, he proceeded to set it ablaze with fire, but it would not catch at all. Deeply perplexed, Shou entered the thicket to search for it.

There he saw a case containing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Beside it, he also saw a deceased monk whose complexion remained unchanged and who had not been consumed by the spreading fire;
this was surely due to the presence of the scripture. One may truly know that scriptures and images are beyond the comprehension of ordinary beings.
Sun Shou personally recounted this.
To the west of the city of Bingzhou in the Tang dynasty, there was a mountain temple named Tongzi. It contained a great image, seated at a height of over one hundred and seventy feet.
The Emperor, who held the Buddhist teachings in profound veneration, visited Bingzhou during the final years of the Xianqing era.

Accompanied by the Empress, he personally came to this temple, as well as to the North Valley, Kaikua, and other sites. The great image stood two hundred feet high; [the Emperor] paid his respects and gazed upon it.

Beholding this, he marveled at its rarity and extraordinary nature. He generously relinquished his precious treasures, wealth, clothing, as well as his consorts and the women of the inner palace, each of whom likewise made sacrifices and renunciations.

Furthermore, he issued an edict to the local officials and magistrates, including Dou Gui and others, ordering them to quickly adorn and embellish the sacred countenance and to ensure that the ground before the niche was made spacious.
On the day of the return to the capital, it was the second year of the Longshuo era.
In the seventh month of autumn, the Inner Office sent out two *kāṣāya* robes, which were dispatched by a palace messenger on horseback to the two temples for their great statues.

On the day the statue at Tongzi Temple was dressed in the *kāṣāya*, it emitted light of five colors from dawn until dusk, its radiance flowing over the cliffs and caves and illuminating the mountains and rivers.
It also entered the small Buddha niche in the Southern Grotto, shining brilliantly throughout the halls. Thousands of monastics and laypeople gazed upon this sight.
Among the myriad people in the city, those of high and low station who beheld this and turned toward goodness numbered seven or eight out of ten households;
this was known to all and required no further words to be fully understood.
In the first year of the Longshuo era of the Tang dynasty, there was a bhikṣuṇī at Jingfu Monastery in Luozhou.

While she was practicing her austerities in her quarters, she had a serving girl named Ren Wuniang. After the girl died, the bhikṣuṇī practiced further austerities and established a spirit altar for Wuniang.

After more than a month had passed, her elder sister and younger brother suddenly heard moaning on the spirit altar during the night. At first, the younger brother was greatly terrified, but later he questioned her.
She replied, "When I was born, I ate meat at the monastery; because of this, I suffer great pain. There are sores upon my body, and I fear they might soil the bedding.
You should place a great deal of ash upon the bed. Her younger brother followed her words and placed the ash there.

Later, he saw that there was a great deal of pus and blood upon the bed. She spoke again to her brother, saying, "I am afflicted by illness and cannot sew clothes. You must [sew] them very roughly..."
"Bring some cloth; I shall make you a shirt and socks. Her younger brother placed the cloth upon the funeral bed, and by dawn it was finished.
He then said to his sister, "When I was a child, I suffered from a lac burn. I once rescued a crab and applied its juice to the wound, which healed.
Now I have entered the Hell of the Forest of Blades, and there are currently seven broken knives within my flesh. I pray that you, my elder sister..."

With compassionate thoughts, he performed meritorious acts to rescue her. Knowing that his sister was in desperate straits and unable to provide for herself, he thought, "The clothing she had on her body at the time of death will be of no benefit to the deceased;
it remains intact even now. I shall request it for her use. Before his sister could reply, he said, "The boy has taken it himself.
After a long while, he spoke again, "The clothes have arrived; they are currently on the bed. His sister then went to look.
This was the attire he had worn when he passed away. He then sent it to Master Bǎoxiàn at Jìngtǔ Temple, entrusting him with the task of transcribing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Each time a scroll was completed, he would report, "One blade has been produced. In this manner, seven scrolls were finished.

He then said, "The seven swords have all been drawn out; now, receiving the aid of blessings, I shall immediately go to take rebirth. He departed after bidding farewell with tears to his elder sister and younger brother.
Shen Xuanfa of Wuxing stated that what the monk Zhizheng of Jingtu Monastery recounted was also the same.
Tang Yao Mingjie was originally a śramaṇa of Puguang Temple. He was by nature intelligent and possessed literary elegance; he was skilled in calligraphy and proficient in painting.
Even in the art of playing the qin, he was peerless among his contemporaries. Yet, he always took pleasure in the mundane world and found no joy in the monastic path.

In the first year of the Longshuo era, he was selected as a candidate for the imperial examination and personally traveled to Luoyang. Upon ascending the rankings and returning to lay life, he adopted the surname Tang.
He spoke several more words before passing away shortly thereafter. Later, he appeared in a dream to his acquaintance, the monk Zhizheng of Jingtu Temple, saying:
"Mingjie lacked merit in his past lives and did not follow the Inner Teachings. Now he undergoes immense suffering and is extremely hungry and destitute.
If you still feel the affection of an old friend, could you perhaps grant him a single meal? Zhizheng gave his word in the dream, and upon waking...
Thereafter, he provided her with food. When it was night and she had just fallen asleep, she immediately saw Mingjie come to express his apologies and thanks.
In the middle of autumn in the second year, she again appeared in a dream to a painter and said, "Because I did not believe in the Buddha-dharma, I am now undergoing great suffering."
He earnestly urged me to compose two or three fascicles of scripture.

Taking my hand, he affectionately composed a poem to bid me farewell, instructing a painter to recite it eighteen times so that I might memorize it; upon waking, I recalled it. The poem says: "Taking hands, we cannot part;

Chest pressed to chest, I grieve for myself. How painful, the brevity of this life’s twilight; How tragic, the long road to the spring path. The pine forest shudders at the wild wind; The desolate earth..."
Falling frost and dew. What gift can parting offer? My thoughts linger upon the chapters of the Inner Canon.
In Yan Village of Wannian County, Tangzhou—which lies between the Ba and Wei Rivers—there was a woman of the Xie family who had married into the Yuan family of the same county.
She had a daughter who married Lai Azhao, a man from Huilong Village. The woman of the Xie family passed away at the end of the Yonghui era.
In the eighth month of the first year of the Longshuo era, [the spirit] appeared in a dream to a woman of the Lai clan and said:

"In my previous life, when selling wine, I used small measures while charging excessive prices; furthermore, I gave short measure of the wine. Because of this sin, I am now a cow in the house of a commoner at the foot of the northern mountain.
Recently, I was sold to the household of Master Xiahou of Fajie Temple. They are now taking me toward the south of the city."
She plowed the rice paddies, enduring great hardship. Upon waking, her daughter wept with tears in her eyes and told Āzhào about it.
In the first month of the second year, a nun from Fajie Monastery arrived at Āzhào’s village. The girl questioned the nun, who replied, "There is a Master Xiahou;
she is indeed your mother. The girl immediately went to the monastery to seek her out. [The nun] said, "Recently, I purchased an ox at the foot of the northern mountain."
She saw that he was currently plowing a field south of the city. The girl wept as she implored a nun from the monastery, who then sent someone to escort her to him.
This ox was normally restrained by only one person; if it encountered anyone else, it would invariably act restive and gore them.
Upon seeing his daughter arrive, he licked her entire body and wept. His daughter then used the funds from Xiahou Shiyu to ransom him, and he followed her away.
He is currently living at the home of A-zhao, where he is being cared for; the daughter constantly calls him "Mother."
His service was never lacking. Many princes, marquises, and their consorts in the capital frequently summoned him to have him gaze upon them, competing to bestow money and silk upon him.
In a village twenty li west of Jiyin County in Caozhou during the Tang dynasty, there was a vihāra.
In the tenth month of winter in the second year of the Longshuo era, a wild fire suddenly broke out with extraordinary ferocity; when it reached the vihāra, it leaped over and passed by.
By that time, the monastic quarters and grass huts had been completely consumed by fire; only one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* remained intact as before.
This was related by Xi Wenli, an aide to the military governor of Caozhou.
In the summer of the second year of the Longshuo era (662 CE), during the fourth month, a fire broke out within the Wuzhong Garrison City in Yuyang County, Youzhou of the Tang dynasty.
Approximately one hundred households were located inside the city walls; the gate towers and the dwellings of the people were all reduced to ashes.
Only two vihāras, a stūpa, and the paper curtains and reed mats atop the Buddha niches remained; wherever there were images of the Buddha, the flames alone did not reach them.

The pyre was set ablaze; yet the fire did not consume it, and it remained standing tall and solitary. Among those who witnessed this at the time, there were none who did not sigh in wonder, attributing it to the sustaining power of the Buddha.
Lang Yuling of Zhongshan, having served as an official there, was also a friend of my elder brother, Yuying.
The Commandant of Qi Prefecture, Yin Ru, was sent on a mission to Yingzhou; he personally witnessed these matters and recounted them in full for the other magistrates.
Ni Mai-de, a native of Qufu in Yanzhou during the Tang dynasty, had a wife named Huangfu who, suffering from illness, prayed at Mount Tai.

Her condition gradually improved, but she was subsequently summoned by the Way of the Netherworld to serve as a "Simit" (an attendant of death). Every time she was dispatched, she would die and then return after one...
On the second day, after the business was concluded, he returned to his former state. He had previously summoned many people;

he himself said that he once sent for the younger daughter of the local military commander Pang Lingjun. Because there was a ritual altar in front of her courtyard where recitations were being performed, she could not enter for a long time.
After a short while, when the recitations were somewhat less busy, and because the candle-bearer happened to go to the sick girl’s location, he then—
He followed them in, and only after a long time was he able to leave. When asked how he had been taken, he said it was by the command of the Prefect’s fourth son;
the Prefect himself did not know. He explained that the hells possess a systematic order.

He further stated that there are many accounts of living people being summoned from beneath the earth, yet because such individuals possess some measure of merit, they cannot be captured. However, if they have committed transgressions, they are seized.
It is easy. Huangfu saw that he was being employed as a servant, which remains the case even today.
As for those who act as "living messengers of death" (sheng siming) among men, there are currently three or four such individuals in Yanzhou, though their names are unknown.

Sima Qiaoqing of Henei, who served as a Judicial Assistant (Sizhi) in the Court of Judicial Review (Dali Si) during the Tang dynasty, was by nature pure and prudent and possessed noble aspirations and conduct.

During the Yonghui era, he served as the District Magistrate for Population and Land Records (Hucu Cao) in Yangzhou. Upon the death of his mother, he observed the mourning period with such physical emaciation that he pierced his chest to draw blood and transcribed one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Not long thereafter, two stalks of *zhicao* (mushroom/herb) grew upon his mourning hut. After nine days had passed—
It was eighteen inches long, with green stalks and crimson caps that exuded one *sheng* of juice daily. Those standing nearby tasted it and found its flavor as sweet as honey;
once the stalk was removed, it grew back again. This occurred four times in succession.
Qiao Qing and several of his colleagues reported this to Yu Ling, and many scholars throughout the world became aware of it.
